text: The game is hide and seek, and the players are the young staff hired to keep everyone else safe. Ninety-three minutes, a New Zealand forest, and a setup that costs nothing to establish and everything to sustain: once people scatter into the trees, the film has to keep finding reasons for them not to come back. Tim McLachlan lets most of the pressure come from social arrangement rather than pursuit, from who pairs off, who gets left behind, which friendship turns out to have been a convenience. Over all of it hangs the sense of being watched by someone, or something, which is the cheapest effect available to a thriller and the hardest to hold past the first hour. The camp does the rest. Under cover of a game, people who are technically in charge revert to the pecking order they were hired to manage.

A career is not a plot, which is the trouble with any film that sets out to tell a life in show business. George M. Cohan's resume alone runs to composer, playwright, actor, dancer and singer, and 126 minutes of ascent will sag unless something holds the numbers in place. Michael Curtiz's version drew Academy attention for editing as well as for acting and directing, which is a fair hint about where the labor went. An editing prize on a musical is a note about seams: where a number starts, how long a film sits in the applause before it moves on. Watch the joins. Songs carry the exposition, stage time and offstage time are cut against each other, and what stands in for a plot is a body of work accumulating. It is a 1942 picture about a man who made things for a living.

In 1788, an English king's body stops being a private matter and becomes a constitutional problem. George III turns confused, then violent, then briefly lucid, and the men around him have to decide whether they are looking at an illness or a vacancy. Nicholas Hytner runs two clocks. One is medical: physicians applying the cures of their day to a condition their profession has no name for. The other is political: Queen Charlotte and William Pitt the Younger counting heads against the Prince of Wales, who has every reason to prefer the graver diagnosis. The comedy lives in the overlap, statecraft conducted at a bedside, medicine practiced on a symbol. Academy attention landed on the lead performance, a supporting performance and the production design, and that last one earns its keep: all that gilding, arranged around one increasingly untidy man.

Rugby league buys a man's body by the season, and Frank Machin decides that is a fair trade. He is hard and quick and wants out of the work otherwise available to him in the north of England around 1960, and the club run by the local employer Weaver is the door that opens. Both leads drew Academy notice, a reasonable signal that the game is not the subject. Lindsay Anderson takes 134 minutes, long for a story about a hard man getting what he asked for, and the surplus is where the film lives: between matches, in rented rooms, at tables, among people unimpressed by a local celebrity. Machin can absorb a beating on a Saturday and cannot manage an ordinary conversation on a Sunday. Being owned by an employer and being adored by a town arrive in the same envelope.

Six stories, six places, and a front line moving north through all of them. Roberto Rossellini follows the Italian Campaign from Sicily to the Po Valley across eighteen months, and the recurring situation is not combat but contact: Americans and Italians on the same side, unable to say so, working through gesture and error and guesswork. Paisa keeps finding new ways for goodwill to arrive garbled. Its Academy recognition went to the screenplay, which sounds odd for a film with this little plot in it and is exactly right: six self-contained pieces, no returning character to stitch the country back together, each ending where it ends. The film was made within a few years of the events it describes, close enough that the question of how much to shape them was still open. It answers by shaping very little.

Charles is offered politics, then religion, then psychoanalysis, and declines all three without raising his voice. It carries a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize, though what Robert Bresson takes seriously here is less the young man's despair than the machinery of consolation built around it: the meetings, the doctrines, the appointments, each with a vocabulary for what is wrong with him and each assuming that being wrong is a condition someone can fix. Ninety-seven minutes, no argument won. There is no conversion to build toward, which leaves the drama somewhere harder to stage: how completely a person can decline what is offered, and how unremarkable that refusal looks from the outside. Charles's disgust is with a decline he reads as moral and physical at once, and the film extends him the courtesy of not diagnosing him.

An ailing novelist, seventy-eight tomorrow, spends a bad night drafting his own family into a book they have not agreed to be in. Clive Langham writes in his head, revises in his head, and breaks in with commentary that is by turns cruel and self-pitying, so the film keeps offering scenes it can withdraw and stage again differently. Alain Resnais made it in English, in 1977, on a structure that leaves no stable ground underfoot: what looks like an event may only be a draft. The comedy is real and it is nasty, since a man in pain has the power to assign his children dialogue. What steadies it is the body. Langham is ill and drinking through the night, and every distortion in the fiction traces back to that pressure, which turns the formal game into something closer to a vigil.

Ra, Culebro, Sere, Winny and Nano: five names, no fixed address between them, and a road out of Medellin. Laura Mora sends them after a promised land, which the film treats as a destination and also as a story the boys tell each other in order to keep walking. What stands to be lost is not comfort, since they have none, but the group: a clan with nothing legal holding it together, no adults, no papers, only the agreement to stay together past the point where staying together is useful. The register slides toward delirium without ever announcing that it has. It carries the Golden Shell and went out as Colombia's submission to the Academy Awards, and across 111 minutes the land the boys cross stops being scenery and starts being the point.

A sweepstakes letter, the kind mailed to everybody, is enough to start an old man walking toward Nebraska. His son does not believe in the prize and drives him anyway, and that transaction is the film: two people with nothing fluent between them, agreeing to sit in a car for a long time. It registered with the Academy in three departments, lead performance, direction and photography. Alexander Payne uses the distance out of Montana to work on what a father owes an explanation for and what a grown child eventually stops asking about, and the joke and the ache turn out to be the same material. A man who has been drinking most of his life will not become legible in 115 minutes. What the film offers instead is proximity, hours of it, on roads that give the two of them nothing to look at but each other.

A train stops at a town that hardly rates one, and a man with one arm steps down onto the platform. What follows is a question of how long Black Rock can keep answering questions with hospitality. John Sturges runs it in eighty-one minutes, and that economy is not modesty: a stranger asking after a name has only so many hours before the town decides what to do with him. The western furniture is present, wide daylight, one main street, distances a person can see across, but the menace here is procedural. Doors close politely. Answers arrive already polished. Macreedy is a veteran with an injury he does not explain and a patience that a guilty town can only read as threat, and the suspense sits in watching for whoever drops the act first.

A novel can break a paragraph and land in another decade; a film has to cut, and the cut has to be legible. That is the problem George Roy Hill took on in 1972, with a man who does not travel through time so much as get moved through it without warning. Billy Pilgrim's childhood, his captivity in Dresden, his suburban middle age and a planet called Tralfamadore all have to belong to one continuous present, with no dream logic to hide behind. The joins carry the argument: for a person who has seen a certain kind of thing, chronology stops being available. It took the Hugo Award, which is science fiction claiming a war picture, and the Directors Guild honored the direction, which is the trade acknowledging how much work those hundred minutes hide.

The house takes in an orphan and never settles on what he is to it: brother, servant, ward, rival. Heathcliff grows up beside Cathy in an arrangement everyone but the two of them treats as provisional, and William Wyler's film is clearest not on the passion but on the accounting, feeling and stature kept in separate books, which is what lets Cathy marry Edgar Linton without believing she has given anything up. His vow to win her back is also a claim on property. It thinks in thresholds: who is inside the house, who waits at the door, who has the standing to cross. In 1939 the Academy singled out the lead performance, the direction and the black-and-white photography, three departments doing one job here, since the story turns on who stands in the light and who is left out in the weather.

Helen leaves for Italy with her married boyfriend, and from that point the London flat is the only location the film needs. Carole stays inside it. Roman Polanski gives her a fear of men that the film never puts up for debate, then lets the apartment carry it: walls, corridors, the ordinary noise of a building with other tenants in it. The first stretch is quiet, a manicurist at work, courteous, elsewhere, wrong in ways that are easy to excuse, and the drift out of that is gradual enough to watch happening, which is the harder thing to stage and the more frightening. A Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize sits on its record. What lingers is how little it required: one woman, one flat, 105 minutes, and almost nothing brought in from outside.

Charm is the engine, and it runs in exactly the way that costs other people something. Alfie moves through London collecting women and calling the whole business an arrangement, and for a long stretch Lewis Gilbert lets him be funny about it, which is the trap. No punishment is staged. What arrives instead is consequence of the ordinary kind: other people's lives continue after he has left the room, and one of them eventually asks more of him than a joke can cover. It drew Academy recognition for the picture, its lead and a supporting performance, and a place on the BFI's hundred British films. A comedy has to keep an audience on the charmer's side, and the discipline here is in how long that stays possible. The tone keeps running while the ground under it is quietly removed.
